title: The Knowledge No One Holds: Vienna, Houghton Street, and the Long Return to Freiburg
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Vienna, birth in the Habsburg capital
stops.date_confidence: attested. Date and city given by the Hoover Institution's Hayek Papers finding aid at the Online Archive of California and by English Wikipedia. No street address for the birth appears in any source consulted, so the pin is central Vienna.
stops.campa: Friedrich August von Hayek is born in Vienna, capital of a monarchy with nineteen years left to live, into a family of physicians, botanists and statisticians who treat the classification of the natural world as ordinary household business. He grows up among herbaria and pressed specimens, in a house where the world arrives already sorted into kinds and somebody in the family has done the sorting. His father August is a municipal doctor who lectures in botany on the side. His mother's father, Franz von Juraschek, is an economist and statistician.
stops.quote: I felt, 'I must be like that, ready for every possibility in life, and be very efficient'
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Hayek, UCLA Oral History Program master transcript (recorded 1978), describing a boyhood ideal modelled on a fireman's horse
suggested_refs: Friedrich A. von Hayek Papers, Hoover Institution Archives, biographical chronology
sources: Online Archive of California finding aid, Friedrich A. von Hayek Papers, Hoover Institution

stops.name: The Isonzo front, the artillery cadet
stops.date_confidence: attested for the March 1917 enlistment and the Italian front service; the exact battery and sector are not pinned by any source consulted, so the coordinates mark the general Isonzo and Piave line where Austro-Hungarian artillery served. A decoration for bravery is reported in biographical accounts but is not securely documented and is not asserted here.
stops.campa: He enters the Austro-Hungarian army in March and goes to the Italian front as an artillery officer cadet, seventeen years old. He says afterward that the war decided his profession: he had seen a whole continent organized by command and wanted to know how any large order holds together at all. The war gives him a malarial illness and takes most of the hearing in his left ear, a deafness that will thicken across seventy-five more years until conversation at a dinner table becomes work. He comes home in 1918 to a state that no longer exists.
suggested_refs: Austro-Hungarian artillery service records for the Isonzo and Piave sectors, 1917-1918
sources: Online Archive of California finding aid, Hoover Institution

stops.name: Vienna, the university in the year the empire ends
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1918 matriculation (Hoover finding aid chronology); the month is an ordering device for the winter semester in the weeks the monarchy dissolved.
stops.campa: He matriculates at the University of Vienna in the winter the Habsburg monarchy is dissolved, a city short of coal, food and currency, its professors lecturing in overcoats. He reads law, because law is where economics is taught, and takes his formation from Friedrich von Wieser, the last of Vienna's founding generation still holding a chair. Inflation is not a topic for a seminar here. It is the price of bread on the walk to the lecture hall, different in the evening from what it was that morning.
suggested_refs: Friedrich von Wieser's Vienna lectures, 1918-1922
sources: Online Archive of California finding aid, Hoover Institution

stops.name: Zurich, the brain-anatomy laboratory
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The laboratory is Constantin von Monakow's brain-anatomy institute, which was in ZURICH, not Vienna: Monakow directed it there from the 1880s until his death in 1930. English Wikipedia names the institute in connection with The Sensory Order but does not place it, and an earlier draft of this file wrongly attached it to the University of Vienna. The visit followed the fuel-shortage closure of the University of Vienna and is placed in 1920; the year is not independently confirmed against a primary record, and the month is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: With the University of Vienna shut for want of fuel, he travels to Zurich and spends weeks in the brain-anatomy laboratory of Constantin von Monakow, tracing fibre bundles through sectioned tissue under a microscope. The question he takes away is not a medical one. If sensation is nothing but a nervous system sorting impulses into classes it has built out of its own past, then a mind is a classifier and not a mirror, and what any one mind holds is a private ordering nobody else can inspect. Thirty-two years later he publishes that thought as a book.
suggested_refs: Constantin von Monakow's Institute of Brain Anatomy, Zurich
Hayek, The Sensory Order (1952), preface on the 1920s origin of the manuscript

stops.name: Vienna, two doctorates in two years
stops.date_confidence: attested for both degrees, Dr. jur. 1921 and Dr. rer. pol. 1923, per the Hoover finding aid chronology. Exact conferral days are not given there; the month here orders the stop. Note the tension flagged in the report: the 1923 political science doctorate falls in the year he sailed for New York in March.
stops.campa: He takes the doctorate in law in 1921 and the doctorate in political science in 1923, both at Vienna, from a faculty that still treats economics as one province of a single moral science rather than as a technique. He has arrived at the field sideways. A lecturer sets out Aristotle's division of practical philosophy into ethics, politics and economics, and he decides on the spot that this is the whole of what he wants to do; he never afterward accepts a border between the three. The two degrees take four years. The fees are a different quantity every term, in a currency worth less each time he pays them.
stops.quote: Well these are the things I want to study
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Hayek, UCLA Oral History Program master transcript (recorded 1978), recalling his reaction to Aristotle's division of practical philosophy; the transcript prints the sentence with a bracketed editorial insertion, 'When I heard this [my response was], "Well these are the things I want to study."'
suggested_refs: University of Vienna doctoral records, Dr. jur. 1921 and Dr. rer. pol. 1923
sources: Online Archive of California finding aid, Hoover Institution
UCLA Oral History Program, Hayek master transcript, static.library.ucla.edu

stops.name: Vienna, the Abrechnungsamt
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the exact terms of the hire and the roughly 1921-1926 span; the employment itself is standard in the biographical record but has not been re-verified here against a primary personnel file. No street address for the office was located, so the pin is central Vienna. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Wieser recommends him to a government office set up to settle the private debts left tangled by the Treaty of Saint-Germain, and the director who hires him is Ludwig von Mises. The office pays in a currency losing value by the week; salaries are revised monthly, then more often than monthly, and the debts Hayek is there to settle are denominated in it. He stays some five years. Mises reads the letter of recommendation, looks at the young man standing in front of him, and remarks that he has never once seen him at his own university lectures.
suggested_refs: The Austrian Abrechnungsamt, the treaty-settlement clearing office under the Treaty of Saint-Germain

stops.name: Vienna, the Geistkreis
stops.date_confidence: attested for the circle, its founding with Herbert Furth and its membership; the founding is dated only to the early 1920s in the sources, so the year and month here order the segment rather than fix an event.
stops.campa: With Herbert Furth he founds a private circle of friends who meet to read papers to one another: Gottfried Haberler, Fritz Machlup, Oskar Morgenstern, Alfred Schutz, Eric Voegelin. They call it the Geistkreis and they refuse it a subject on purpose, taking economics one evening and art history or jurisprudence the next, on the principle that no one of them should be permitted to become only an economist. It runs into the 1930s and then scatters, most of its members to American universities.
suggested_refs: The Geistkreis membership rolls, reconstructed in Hayek's UCLA oral history
sources: UCLA Oral History Program, Hayek master transcript

stops.name: Vienna, the private seminar every other Friday
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hayek was a regular of the Mises Privatseminar, which ran across the 1920s until 1934. The date is an ordering device, not a start date; the seminar has no single documented first meeting. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from ludwig_von_mises.journey.json.
stops.campa: Mises holds a seminar every other Friday evening in his office at the Chamber of Commerce, by invitation, with no fees, no examinations and no university standing whatever. Hayek is among the regulars, with Machlup, Morgenstern, Schutz and Voegelin; the evening moves on to an Italian restaurant and then to the Cafe Kunstler, and the argument runs into the small hours. Hayek is never a converted Misesian and says so plainly. What he learns from Mises first are the conclusions, and only much later the reasoning.
stops.quote: I just learned he was usually right in his conclusions, but I was not completely satisfied with his argument.
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Hayek, UCLA Oral History Program master transcript (recorded 1978), on his early relationship with Ludwig von Mises
suggested_refs: The Mises Privatseminar, Vienna Chamber of Commerce, c. 1920-1934
sources: UCLA Oral History Program, Hayek master transcript

stops.name: New York, assistant to Jeremiah Jenks
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, drawn from the dossier's reading of Rockefeller Archive Center material naming March 1923 to June 1924; the Rockefeller overview page was named but not independently refetched in this pass. Coordinates mark NYU's Washington Square campus, though he also attended classes at Columbia in Morningside Heights during the same stretch.
stops.campa: He arrives in New York in March with almost no money and works as research assistant to Jeremiah W. Jenks at New York University, collecting Federal Reserve series. For fifteen months he sits in on classes at NYU and at Columbia, where he hears Wesley Clair Mitchell on the business cycle. American economics is empirical, institutional, statistical, everything Vienna is not, and he takes the measurements seriously and the explanations not at all. He sails home in June 1924 and goes back to his desk at the clearing office.
suggested_refs: Rockefeller Foundation fellowship files on economics research funding, Rockefeller Archive Center
sources: Rockefeller Archive Center, 'Understanding the Business Cycle' (named in dossier, not refetched)

stops.name: Vienna, the institute for business cycle research
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hayek and Mises founded the Osterreichisches Institut fur Konjunkturforschung and that Hayek became its first director; the sources conflict on whether the founding falls at the end of 1926 or in 1927, a conflict flagged in ludwig_von_mises.journey.json and left unresolved here. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from that file.
stops.campa: At the end of 1926 he and Mises found the Austrian Institute for Business Cycle Research, and in 1927 Hayek becomes its first director, twenty-eight years old, running a forecasting shop on a Rockefeller Foundation subsidy in a small republic that has already had one currency destroyed inside his adult memory. The institute publishes monthly indices; its director spends his own hours on the theory of why the indices move at all. He hands the desk to Oskar Morgenstern when he leaves for London.
suggested_refs: WIFO institutional history of the Osterreichisches Institut fur Konjunkturforschung
sources: WIFO institutional history (wifo.ac.at, cited in dossier, not independently refetched)

stops.name: Vienna, Privatdozent and the first book
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1929 Habilitation and Privatdozent appointment (Hoover finding aid). The publication of Geldtheorie und Konjunkturtheorie in the same year is carried from the standard bibliographic record and was not refetched from a library catalogue. Month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He completes his Habilitation and becomes a lecturer in economics at the University of Vienna, and publishes Geldtheorie und Konjunkturtheorie: the argument that credit expansion unbacked by saving distorts the whole structure of production through time, and that a boom therefore carries its own bust inside it from the first day. English readers will not have it for another four years, as Monetary Theory and the Trade Cycle. He is thirty when it comes out, and it comes out in the year the New York market breaks.
suggested_refs: Hayek, Geldtheorie und Konjunkturtheorie (Vienna, 1929), translated as Monetary Theory and the Trade Cycle (1933)
sources: Online Archive of California finding aid, Hoover Institution

stops.name: London School of Economics, the four lectures
stops.date_confidence: attested that the four lectures were given at Robbins's invitation in early 1931 and published the same year as Prices and Production; the precise lecture dates within January and February are not fixed in the sources consulted. Coordinates are the LSE Houghton Street pin as carried in george_soros.journey.json.
stops.campa: Lionel Robbins invites him to give four lectures at the London School of Economics, and Hayek arrives with an English learned largely from reading, to deliver an account of capital as a structure of stages laid out in time that his audience has never encountered. The room does not follow all of it and is gripped anyway. The lectures are published within the year as Prices and Production, with the diagrams of the production structure that everybody will come to call Hayekian triangles, and a visiting appointment follows inside twelve months.
suggested_refs: Hayek, Prices and Production (London, 1931)
The Old Building, Houghton Street, opened 1922

stops.name: London School of Economics, the review and Sraffa's answer
stops.date_confidence: attested and corrected here. Hayek's review of Keynes's Treatise on Money ran in Economica in two parts, August 1931 and February 1932. Piero Sraffa's 'Dr. Hayek on Money and Capital' appeared in the Economic Journal in 1932 (42: 42-53), with a rejoinder in June 1932, and its target was Prices and Production rather than the Treatise review. An earlier draft compressed the whole exchange into 1931; it spans 1931-1932. Keynes's 'frightful muddle' remark is widely quoted and was not re-verified against a primary Keynes text in this pass.
stops.campa: In August the first part of his review of Keynes's Treatise on Money appears in Economica, hard and unsparing; Keynes answers in kind and calls Prices and Production a frightful muddle. The following year Piero Sraffa takes the capital theory apart in the Economic Journal, and it is capital, the inheritance from Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk, that proves to be the weak joint. When the General Theory comes in 1936 Hayek does not review it. He calls that a regret afterward. Why he stayed silent at the one moment his answer would have been read, no account he ever gave quite explains.
suggested_refs: Piero Sraffa, 'Dr. Hayek on Money and Capital', Economic Journal 42 (1932), 42-53
Hayek, 'Reflections on the Pure Theory of Money of Mr. J. M. Keynes', Economica, August 1931 and February 1932

stops.name: London School of Economics, the Tooke chair
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1932 election to the Tooke Professorship of Economic Science and Statistics and for its tenure to 1950 (Hoover finding aid); the month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He is elected Tooke Professor of Economic Science and Statistics, and for a few seasons he is the principal rival to Cambridge in English economics. Students come to London for him, and he lectures in an English learned largely from books. Then the argument turns, the young go over to Keynes almost as a body, and Hayek finds himself at forty holding a chair in a subject that has moved without him. He does not change his position. He holds the chair for eighteen years, until he resigns it in 1950 for a temporary post in Arkansas.
suggested_refs: The Tooke Professorship of Economic Science and Statistics, University of London
sources: Online Archive of California finding aid, Hoover Institution

stops.name: Vienna, the collected Menger
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hayek edited the four-volume Gesammelte Werke of Carl Menger, printed 1933-1936, restoring the unrevised 1871 text of the Grundsatze; carl_menger.journey.json carries the detail at reconstruction level after a Mises Institute page returned 404, and flags it as worth re-verifying. The Vienna pin, inherited from that file, marks Menger's city and the printing; Hayek himself held the Tooke chair in London throughout these years and did the editorial work from there.
stops.campa: He edits the four volumes of Carl Menger's collected works for the London School's reprint series, restoring the unrevised 1871 text of the Grundsatze, the book that began the Austrian school and that Menger's own later revisions had blurred. It is an act of custody rather than authorship: fixing a founder's text at the moment it was first right, at a distance of sixty years and a national border, while the city that produced it moves year by year toward the Anschluss. The volumes are printed between 1933 and 1936.
suggested_refs: Carl Menger, Gesammelte Werke, ed. F. A. Hayek, 4 vols. (London School of Economics reprint series, 1933-1936)

stops.name: London School of Economics, the calculation debate and the knowledge problem
stops.date_confidence: attested for Collectivist Economic Planning (1935) and 'Economics and Knowledge' (1937) as publications; both are carried from the standard bibliographic record rather than refetched, and the single 1935 date orders a stop that covers two years of one argument.
stops.campa: He edits Collectivist Economic Planning, putting Mises's argument that a socialist economy cannot calculate in front of an English readership that has never seen it, and Oskar Lange answers with a model of market socialism that claims to solve the problem on paper. Two years later Hayek reads Economics and Knowledge to the London Economic Club and moves the ground under both sides. The objection is no longer that planners lack incentives. It is that the knowledge a planner would need does not exist anywhere in one place, and cannot.
suggested_refs: Hayek, ed., Collectivist Economic Planning (1935)
Hayek, 'Economics and Knowledge', Economica (1937)

stops.name: London, naturalized British subject
stops.date_confidence: year attested, day NOT confirmed. The Hoover finding aid chronology reads only '1938 - Naturalized as British subject', and English Wikipedia says only that Hayek and his children became British subjects in 1938. The precise date 18 July 1938 circulates in the dossier but is unverified against a naturalisation certificate, so the stop is dated to the year and the month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: In 1938 Hayek and his children become British subjects. Austria has been annexed in March; the country whose passport he holds has stopped existing for the second time inside his own lifetime, and this time there is no going back to it. He is thirty-nine. He keeps the German of his childhood, writes in English from here on, and will be called an Austrian economist for the rest of his career by people who mean it as a school and not as a nationality. He had already written down, five years before, what he thought collectivism does once it is let in anywhere.
stops.quote: the inherent logic of collectivism makes it impossible to confine it to a limited sphere
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Hayek, 'Nazi-Socialism' memorandum, spring 1933, quoted in Bruce Caldwell's introduction to The Road to Serfdom: The Definitive Edition (University of Chicago Press, 2007). NOT a line from The Road to Serfdom itself, as it is often cited.
suggested_refs: Hayek naturalisation certificate, 1938, United Kingdom
Hayek, 'Nazi-Socialism' memorandum, spring 1933, Hayek Papers
sources: Online Archive of California finding aid, Hoover Institution

stops.name: Paris, the Colloque Walter Lippmann
stops.date_confidence: attested for August 1938 and for Hayek's presence alongside Mises, Ropke, Rustow, Rougier and Lippmann, per ludwig_von_mises.journey.json. The venue was not pinned more precisely in that file either; coordinates are the Paris centroid, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: Louis Rougier gathers a few dozen people in Paris for five days around Walter Lippmann's book, to ask whether liberalism can be rebuilt rather than merely defended in retreat. Hayek is there with Mises, Wilhelm Ropke, Alexander Rustow, Raymond Aron, Jacques Rueff. A word is coined in the room for what they are attempting: neoliberalism, and no two of them mean the same thing by it. Then they disagree about nearly everything that matters, how much state, what kind of law, whether the nineteenth century is a model or a warning, and go home in the last August before the war.
suggested_refs: Colloque Walter Lippmann, Paris, August 1938, proceedings

stops.name: Peterhouse, Cambridge, the war years
stops.date_confidence: attested that the LSE decamped to Cambridge and was housed in Peterhouse buildings, and that Hayek worked and wrote there through the war; his personal Cambridge residence address was not located, and the fire-watching detail is a widely repeated recollection rather than a documented duty roster. The month orders the start of the wartime term.
stops.campa: The School of Economics evacuates to Cambridge and Keynes finds his rival rooms at Peterhouse, his own college. They spend the war as friendly neighbours, taking turns on a college roof at night watching for incendiaries, arguing across a table about the question the war is going to settle without either of them. Hayek gives the days to a book he calls the Abuse of Reason, an attempt to trace where the idea of engineering a whole society came from. He never finishes it. He pulls one section out of it instead.
suggested_refs: The unfinished 'Abuse of Reason' project, Hayek Papers, Hoover Institution

stops.name: London, Routledge publishes The Road to Serfdom
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 10 March 1944 British publication by Routledge (University of Chicago Press publication-history page, fetched directly). Coordinates approximate Routledge's historic London offices near Fleet Street; a precise 1944 street address was not confirmed. The printed dedication reads 'To the socialists of all parties'; the phrasing 'dedicated to socialists of all parties' that circulates is a paraphrase.
stops.campa: Routledge publishes the extracted section on the tenth of March, the work of a technical economist who expects a few hundred colleagues to read it. The argument is that central planning cannot be confined to economic life, and that the country now at war with Germany has been quietly borrowing the habits of thought that produced it. The first printing is two thousand copies and sells out inside a month. Paper rationing keeps it scarce for the duration; Hayek takes to calling it that unobtainable book.
stops.quote: To the socialists of all parties
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Hayek, The Road to Serfdom (Routledge, 1944), dedication page, as printed
suggested_refs: The Road to Serfdom, first Routledge printing, London, March 1944

stops.name: Chicago, the American edition
stops.date_confidence: attested. The University of Chicago Press publication-history page (fetched directly) gives manuscript acceptance on 28 December 1943, publication on 18 September 1944, three prior American rejections, Aaron Director's advocacy, and the complete resetting of the text because the British edition's 'this country' meant England.
stops.campa: Three American publishers have already refused the manuscript, one of them calling it unsuited to the American market. Aaron Director presses it on the University of Chicago Press, which accepts it in December and resets the entire text, because a book written in England says this country and means England. It appears on the eighteenth of September and makes a public figure of a man who has been to the United States twice. The Book of the Month Club takes it; the reprints pass a million.
suggested_refs: University of Chicago Press files on the 1944 American edition of The Road to Serfdom

stops.name: New York, the lecture tour and the condensations
stops.date_confidence: attested and corrected here. The Look magazine cartoon version appeared in FEBRUARY 1945, before the April 1945 Reader's Digest condensation, and was later distributed as a pamphlet by General Motors; an earlier draft reversed the order. The figure of roughly 8,750,000 is Reader's Digest's circulation, not a Book-of-the-Month Club readership. The tour crossed the country; the New York pin marks its point of arrival rather than a single venue.
stops.campa: Look magazine runs a cartoon version in February, later handed out as a pamphlet by General Motors. Reader's Digest condenses the book to twenty pages in April, into a circulation of eight and three quarter million. Hayek lands for a short academic tour and finds it converted into a speaking circuit across the country, in front of businessmen who have read the cartoon and want a champion. He tells them, over and over, that he is not against government activity as such and that they must stop arguing as though he were.
stops.quote: I think what is needed is a clear set of principles which enables us to distinguish between the legitimate fields of government activities and the illegitimate fields of government activity. You must cease to argue for and against government activity as such.
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Hayek, remarks before business groups on the April 1945 American lecture tour, quoted in Bruce Caldwell's introduction to The Road to Serfdom: Text and Documents, The Definitive Edition (University of Chicago Press, 2007)
suggested_refs: Look magazine, February 1945, cartoon version of The Road to Serfdom
Reader's Digest, April 1945, twenty-page condensation

stops.name: London School of Economics, the use of knowledge in society
stops.date_confidence: attested as a September 1945 American Economic Review article (35:4); the essay is carried from the standard bibliographic record and the opening sentence was confirmed against the Library of Economics and Liberty full text. The month is the issue month, not a datable event in London.
stops.campa: In the September American Economic Review he publishes twelve pages under the title The Use of Knowledge in Society. The economic problem of a society, he argues, is not the allocation of given resources, because the givens are not given to anybody: knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place exists only in dispersed, contradictory, perishable scraps held by people who could not state what they know if asked. A price is therefore not a measurement. It is a signal that lets a man who knows nothing whatever about Bolivian tin do the right thing about tin.
stops.quote: What is the problem we wish to solve when we try to construct a rational economic order?
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Hayek, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society', American Economic Review 35:4 (September 1945), opening sentence
suggested_refs: Hayek, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society', AER 35:4 (1945), 519-530

stops.name: Mont Pelerin, the society founded
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 10 April 1947 founding, the thirty-nine invited participants, and Hayek as founding president (dates of his presidency given as 1947-1961 by English Wikipedia and 1947-1962 by the Hoover finding aid, a conflict left unresolved). Coordinates inherited byte-identical from ludwig_von_mises.journey.json; an earlier draft placed the mountain about five kilometres southeast of its true position.
stops.campa: Thirty-nine scholars and journalists come up the mountain above Vevey to the Hotel du Parc for ten days of argument, paid for by a Swiss organizer and an American foundation: Mises, Karl Popper, Milton Friedman, George Stigler, Wilhelm Ropke, Frank Knight. Hayek convenes them and is made president. He wants no party and no programme, only a room in which a defeated position can be thought through again by people who will not be laughed out of it. The first session nearly breaks apart over the income tax.
suggested_refs: Mont Pelerin Society founding statement, 10 April 1947
The Hotel du Parc, Mont Pelerin, commune of Chardonne, above Vevey

stops.name: Fayetteville, Arkansas, the residency and the divorce
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1950 Arkansas visiting professorship (Hoover finding aid), the Arkansas divorce, and the remarriage to Helene Bitterlich the same year. The conduct of the divorce, including the concealment and financial pressure documented in Caldwell and Klausinger's biography, is reported in specialist scholarship not independently refetched here. The month orders the spring term; the divorce is placed in July by the biographical record.
stops.campa: Hella will not agree to a divorce and English law will not grant him one against her. He takes a temporary professorship at the University of Arkansas because Arkansas will, resigns the chair he has held for eighteen years, and obtains the decree in July. Within weeks he marries Helene Bitterlich, whom he had wanted to marry in 1926 and had not. He says almost nothing about any of it afterward, in a life otherwise spent on the rules that hold people to one another. Lionel Robbins stops speaking to him for years, and his children are estranged.
suggested_refs: Bruce Caldwell and Hansjorg Klausinger, Hayek: A Life, 1899-1950 (2022), on the Arkansas divorce
sources: Online Archive of California finding aid, Hoover Institution

stops.name: Chicago, the Committee on Social Thought
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1950-1962 appointment as Professor of Social and Moral Science on the Committee on Social Thought, and for the ten-year financing of the salary by the William Volker Fund (Hoover finding aid; Volker financing corroborated by scholarship cited in the dossier but not refetched here). The economics department's refusal is standard in the record and is reported rather than documented here. Month orders the autumn quarter.
stops.campa: The Chicago economics department will not have him: his capital theory is out of favour, and the department votes him down. He is appointed instead to the Committee on Social Thought, as Professor of Social and Moral Science, with the salary paid for ten years by the William Volker Fund rather than by the university itself. He is fifty-one, in a new country, married to a new wife, holding a post that is not in his own discipline. He treats the arrangement as freedom. After 1950 he writes almost no technical economics again.
suggested_refs: William Volker Fund records, Rubenstein Library, Duke University
sources: Online Archive of California finding aid, Hoover Institution

stops.name: Chicago, The Sensory Order
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1952 publication; the claim that the manuscript was first conceived in the 1920s is Hayek's own account, carried from the standard bibliographic record rather than refetched. Month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He takes out the manuscript he drafted as a student and finishes it: a theory of mind in which the nervous system is a classifying apparatus that builds its own map of the world by linkage, so that sensory qualities are positions in that map rather than properties of anything outside it. No brain can fully explain itself, he argues, because an explaining system must be more complex than what it explains. It is the knowledge problem run on one skull instead of on a society. Psychologists ignore the book for decades.
suggested_refs: Hayek, The Sensory Order: An Inquiry into the Foundations of Theoretical Psychology (1952)
sources: Online Archive of California finding aid, Hoover Institution

stops.name: London, the institute Antony Fisher builds instead
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Institute of Economic Affairs, founded 1955 in Westminster by Antony Fisher with Oliver Smedley, and for Hayek's advice to Fisher to build a research institution rather than enter politics. Fisher's approach to Hayek dates from 1945-46, not 1955; the stop is dated to the founding. Coordinates corrected here to 2 Lord North Street, Westminster; an earlier draft placed the institute half a kilometre away near Buckingham Palace Road.
stops.campa: A young RAF veteran named Antony Fisher had come to him at the School of Economics after reading the Reader's Digest condensation, asking whether he should go into politics. Hayek told him not to. Politics follows opinion, opinion follows the people who supply the ideas, and the work is to reach what he called the second-hand dealers in ideas. Fisher went away and made a fortune in broiler chickens. Roughly a decade after that conversation he founds the Institute of Economic Affairs at 2 Lord North Street in Westminster, with Oliver Smedley.
suggested_refs: Institute of Economic Affairs, 2 Lord North Street, Westminster, founded 1955

stops.name: Obergurgl, the summers in the Otztal
stops.date_confidence: attested as a recurring habit across the 1950s to the 1970s rather than a single dated visit; no individual stay is pinned in the sources, so the date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: He is a serious mountain walker well into old age, and he works on the mountain, which is to say he stops writing and keeps thinking. The habit outlasts three nationalities and two continents of employment; when his health finally forbids him the altitude, he counts that among the real losses of getting old. Summer after summer through the Chicago and Freiburg and Salzburg years he comes back to the same Tyrolean village at the head of the Otztal, puts on the boots, and goes up past the last of the tree line.
suggested_refs: Obergurgl, Otztal, Tyrol, Hayek's recurring summer retreat

stops.name: Chicago, The Constitution of Liberty
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1960 publication (Hoover Institution biographical page, fetched directly). The detail that he finished it on his sixtieth birthday is a standard biographical report, not independently documented here. Month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Ten years of the Committee produce a book that is not economics at all: an account of freedom as the absence of coercion by another man's arbitrary will, of the rule of law as general rules known in advance and binding on the lawgiver too, and of the case for limits that may not be suspended for a good reason. He is sixty when he finishes it. It is the book a British prime minister will one day pull out of her bag and bang on a table, and the same book he posts, two years after publication, to a dictator in Lisbon.
suggested_refs: Hayek, The Constitution of Liberty (University of Chicago Press, 1960)

stops.name: Freiburg, the chair in economic policy
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1962-1968 as Professor of Economic Policy at the Albert-Ludwigs-Universitat Freiburg, per the Hoover finding aid and German Wikipedia. An earlier draft dated the retirement to 1967; both institutional records give 1968, with 1967-68 as the academic year of transition. Month orders the summer semester.
stops.campa: He returns to Europe at sixty-three, to a chair in economic policy at Freiburg in the Black Forest, in the country of the ordoliberals around Walter Eucken who had set out to plan the constitution of a market rather than the market itself. The German pension arrangements are better than the American ones, which matters to a man supporting two households and holding no capital. He teaches there six years. He also begins the long systematic book on law that will take him another seventeen to finish.
suggested_refs: Albert-Ludwigs-Universitat Freiburg, chair in economic policy, 1962-1968
sources: Online Archive of California finding aid, Hoover Institution

stops.name: Freiburg, the copy sent to Salazar
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The letter and its date of 8 July 1962 are carried from Farrant and McPhail's study as cited in the dossier; that study was named but not independently refetched in this pass, and the wording of the covering note is reported rather than quoted from the original here.
stops.campa: On the eighth of July he sends a copy of The Constitution of Liberty to Antonio de Oliveira Salazar in Lisbon, with a note hoping the Portuguese dictator will find in it useful sketches toward a constitution that could guard against the abuses of democracy. Salazar has ruled for three decades by then, through a secret police and a censorship office. The book argues that the rule of law means general rules binding on whoever makes them. He posts it to a man for whom law is an instrument held in one hand.
suggested_refs: Andrew Farrant and Edward McPhail, on Hayek's 1962 letter to Salazar

stops.name: Los Angeles, the Flint professorship
stops.date_confidence: attested for the visiting Flint Professorship of Philosophy at UCLA in 1968-1969 (Hoover Institution biographical page). Month orders the academic year. The 1978 UCLA oral history recorded a decade later belongs to the same institutional relationship.
stops.campa: He spends a year at the University of California at Los Angeles as visiting Flint Professor of Philosophy, running seminars on the philosophy of the social sciences for graduate students, in a room small enough that his deafness is not yet a barrier. He is sixty-nine and thoroughly out of fashion among economists, and the department that has him is not economics. The material becomes the first volume of Law, Legislation and Liberty. A decade later UCLA comes back to record him for its oral history of Nobel laureates.
suggested_refs: UCLA Oral History Program, Nobel Laureates interviews, Hayek transcript (recorded 1978)

stops.name: Salzburg, the library too small
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Salzburg appointment 1969-1977; the depression of roughly 1969-1974 and Hayek's later judgment that the move was a mistake are reported in biographical accounts not independently refetched here, and are carried at reconstruction level. Month orders the winter semester.
stops.campa: He takes a chair at Salzburg to be back in Austria and regrets it almost at once: a small department, a library that cannot supply what he needs, students who are not the students of London or Chicago. A depression settles on him and stays for years. He is past seventy, he believes his work is finished and unread, and he cannot get the second volume of the book on law to move at all. He calls the move to Salzburg, afterward, the great mistake of his life.
suggested_refs: University of Salzburg, Hayek's chair, 1969-1977

stops.name: Salzburg, Law, Legislation and Liberty
stops.date_confidence: attested for the three volumes dated 1973-1979 (Hoover Institution biographical page). The first volume is dated to the year, not to a documented publication day; month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The first volume appears, and the distinction it turns on is Greek in its vocabulary and entirely his own in its use: nomos, the law that is found, grown out of the practice of people settling disputes one at a time, and thesis, the law that is made, the command of a legislature aimed at a particular purpose. A parliament asked to do both at once, he argues, cannot help destroying the first with the second. Three volumes run from 1973 to 1979. He begins them convinced nobody is reading him.
suggested_refs: Hayek, Law, Legislation and Liberty, 3 vols. (1973-1979)

stops.name: Stockholm, the prize shared with Myrdal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1974 joint award to Hayek and Gunnar Myrdal and for the 10 December Stockholm ceremony. Coordinates corrected here to the Stockholm Concert Hall's own position; an earlier draft placed the venue about three hundred metres southeast. The detail that Hayek took the telephone call for a joke is reported, not documented.
stops.campa: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences goes jointly to Hayek and to Gunnar Myrdal, a Swedish social democrat and an architect of the welfare state, for pioneering work on money and economic fluctuations and for penetrating analysis of the interdependence of economic, social and institutional phenomena. Neither man is pleased with the pairing. Hayek has been out of professional economics for twenty years and out of fashion for forty. At the banquet that evening he tells the room what he thinks of the prize he has just accepted. Myrdal will later argue that it ought to be abolished altogether.
stops.quote: I must confess that if I had been consulted whether to establish a Nobel Prize in economics, I should have decidedly advised against it.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Friedrich Hayek's Nobel banquet speech, Stockholm, 10 December 1974. Reconstruction: nobelprize.org returned HTTP 403 to every fetch attempt in this pass, so the wording is carried from a secondary aggregation and not confirmed against the primary transcript.
suggested_refs: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences press release, 1974 Prize in Economic Sciences
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences'

stops.name: Stockholm, The Pretence of Knowledge
stops.date_confidence: attested for the lecture and its title; the 11 December date is carried from the Nobel Foundation's own lecture page, which returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch in this pass and was read through a text proxy. The banquet remark about advising against the prize is reported at reconstruction level: the primary transcript at nobelprize.org could not be reached to confirm its exact wording.
stops.campa: The day after the ceremony he gives the lecture, and uses it to attack the discipline that has just honoured him. Economics has borrowed the dignity of the physical sciences by imitating their procedures, measuring what can be measured and treating the rest as unreal, and the inflation and unemployment now running together across the West are the harvest of advice given with an authority nobody ever had. The prize itself, he had said at the banquet the night before, confers on one man a standing that in economics no man ought to possess.
stops.quote: To act on the belief that we possess the knowledge and the power which enable us to shape the processes of society entirely to our liking, knowledge which in fact we do not possess, is likely to make us do much harm.
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Hayek, Nobel Memorial Lecture 'The Pretence of Knowledge', Stockholm, 11 December 1974
suggested_refs: Hayek, 'The Pretence of Knowledge', Nobel Memorial Lecture, 11 December 1974

stops.name: Santiago, twenty minutes with Pinochet
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hayek visited Chile in 1977, met General Pinochet, and accepted an honorary link with the Centro de Estudios Publicos. The character of the meeting, roughly twenty minutes with no interpreter and little substantive discussion, comes from Caldwell and Montes's study, which returned 403 to direct fetch in this pass. No month is documented; the date orders the segment. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from augusto_pinochet.journey.json; that file carries no reciprocal stop for the visit.
stops.campa: He comes to Chile at the invitation of a business school and is received by General Augusto Pinochet for about twenty minutes, without an interpreter, with little said on either side. The regime is four years old and has by then killed, disappeared and tortured thousands of its own citizens. Hayek accepts an honorary association with a Santiago research centre and leaves. He is seventy-eight years old, the most famous living defender of the rule of law, and he has just sat down with a man who suspended it.
suggested_refs: Bruce Caldwell and Leonidas Montes, 'Friedrich Hayek and his visits to Chile' (SSRN)

stops.name: Vienna, remembering cousin Ludwig
stops.date_confidence: attested for the essay 'Remembering My Cousin Ludwig Wittgenstein' (1977) and for the kinship through the Juraschek line. The wartime meeting on the train is Hayek's own recollection and is documented nowhere else; the month is an ordering device, and the Vienna pin marks the family's city rather than a place Hayek travelled to for this.
stops.campa: He publishes a short memoir of his second cousin Ludwig Wittgenstein. The two branches of the family meet through the Juraschek line, and the two men spend their working lives circling the same question from opposite ends, which is what language can and cannot be made to carry. Hayek read the Tractatus as soon as it appeared and once thought of writing the biography. They met by chance on a train home from the Italian front, two young Viennese officers in uniform, and afterward only occasionally. That train is Hayek's own recollection and stands in no other record.
suggested_refs: Hayek, 'Remembering My Cousin Ludwig Wittgenstein' (1977)

stops.name: Stanford, the Hoover fellowship
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Hoover Institution fellowship from 1977 and for the archive as the eventual home of his papers. Extent corrected here: the current Online Archive of California finding aid gives 173 manuscript boxes and 91 linear feet, together with oversize, card file, folio boxes, trays, folders, sound cassettes and 1,395 digital files; an earlier draft carried a stale figure of 90.8 linear feet in 172 boxes. Coordinates corrected to the Hoover Institution's own position. Month orders the segment.
stops.campa: He becomes an honorary fellow of the Hoover Institution at Stanford, which will end by holding his papers: diaries, correspondence, drafts, the working files of the Mont Pelerin Society. A hundred and seventy-three manuscript boxes, ninety-one linear feet, with card files, folio boxes, sound cassettes and 1,395 digital files. The man who spent sixty years arguing that no single point can hold the knowledge a society runs on leaves his own in one building in California. Parts of it are still closed to readers.

stops.name: Santiago, the interview in El Mercurio
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1981 return to Chile and the El Mercurio interview; the transcript itself returned 403 to direct fetch in this pass, and the substance is corroborated through translated extracts cited in the dossier and wide secondary discussion. No exact day is documented; the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: Back in Chile, he tells El Mercurio that he opposes dictatorship as a permanent institution but can accept it as a transitional arrangement, and that he would personally prefer a liberal dictator to a democratic government lacking in liberalism. He says this inside a country under military rule, to the newspaper that helped bring that rule about, while the disappearances are still being counted. The sentence is quoted against him in every hostile account written since. He never retracts it.

stops.name: Freiburg, The Fatal Conceit
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1988 publication. The quoted sentence is traced to chapter 5, page 76, by Econlib and carried as the subtitle of a Routledge monograph; the words and page cite were confirmed in scholarly secondary sources, not in a page image of the 1988 edition. The claim circulating elsewhere that the line is an epigraph to some editions of The Road to Serfdom is unsupported and is dropped here.
stops.campa: At eighty-nine he publishes his last book, on the extended order of human cooperation as something grown rather than designed, on morals as rules that spread because the groups keeping them survived and not because anyone reasoned them out, and on the belief that a mind can design what only a long selection produced. He entered the subject by way of Aristotle and leaves it writing about tradition, selection and the limits of what anyone can know. The sentence everybody takes away from the book sits in chapter five, on page seventy-six.
stops.quote: The curious task of economics is to demonstrate to men how little they really know about what they imagine they can design.
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Hayek, The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism (1988), ch. 5, p. 76

stops.name: Freiburg, the medal he cannot travel to receive
stops.date_confidence: the 1991 award of the Presidential Medal of Freedom by George H. W. Bush is attested by the Hoover Institution biographical page; the detail that Hayek was too frail to travel is reported in the dossier and not independently refetched. No exact ceremony day is carried here, so the month orders the segment. He was never physically present at the Washington ceremony, and the stop sits at his Freiburg pin for that reason.
stops.campa: George H. W. Bush awards him the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and he is too frail to cross the Atlantic to take it. He is ninety-two, deaf, and has watched in the previous two years the whole eastern half of the continent he was born in abandon the planned economy he spent sixty years arguing against. The medal is conferred in a room in Washington that he never enters. He makes no public claim of vindication, and the record does not preserve what he said about it at home.

stops.name: Freiburg, death at ninety-two
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and place, corroborated by English Wikipedia, the Hoover Institution page and the Hoover finding aid. The cause of death is reported in the contemporary press as a heart ailment; the Washington Post obituary of 25 March 1992 returned 403 to direct fetch in this pass, and no certified cause is in the reachable record.
stops.campa: He dies at home in Freiburg on the twenty-third of March, ninety-two years old. Contemporary reporting gives a heart ailment; no certified cause is anywhere in the reachable record. He was born a subject of Franz Joseph and fought in the last war the Habsburg empire ever waged. He was famous at forty-five, forgotten at sixty, and given the highest prize in his field at seventy-five. The Washington Post runs its obituary two days later, on the twenty-fifth.

stops.name: Neustifter Friedhof, Vienna, group one, row seventeen
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 4 April 1992 burial and the grave plot Gruppe 1, Reihe 17, Nummer 11, per German Wikipedia. Coordinates corrected here to the Neustifter Friedhof itself at Potzleinsdorfer Hohe 2 in Vienna's eighteenth district, Wahring; earlier drafts pinned the neighbouring locality of Neustift am Walde and assigned the cemetery to the nineteenth district. The Catholic rite is attested; the deathbed-conversion story that circulates has no reliable evidence behind it and is tagged as tradition, not fact.
stops.campa: He is brought back to Vienna and buried on the fourth of April in the Neustifter cemetery on the Potzleinsdorfer Hohe, according to the Catholic rite: group one, row seventeen, number eleven. He had been an agnostic since about the age of fifteen and never took it back; the retellings that turn the Catholic burial into a deathbed conversion have nothing whatever behind them. The city he left for London in 1931 lists the grave among its honorary graves, one of forty-nine in that ground.
